questions.q: In a full-reload pipeline, what does the nightly job actually reprocess to pick up one new day's transactions?
options: The entire accumulated history in bronze.sales_raw, not just the new day
Only the rows from the single new day, nothing else
A random 10% sample of historical data
Only the rows that failed validation the previous night
questions.explain: The full-reload design reads and rebuilds from the entire accumulated history every night, even though only one day's worth of rows is actually new.

questions.q: According to this lesson's core principle, what does runtime and cost scale with in a full-reload design?
options: Total accumulated history, not what's actually new
The number of Regional Managers using the Gold tables
The number of columns in bronze.sales_raw
The size of the Power BI report connected to Gold
questions.explain: The lesson states the core principle directly: in a full-reload design, runtime and compute cost scale with total accumulated history, not with what's actually new.

questions.q: Why does the nightly job's runtime keep growing even if day-to-day transaction volume is completely flat?
options: Because the amount of old history the job insists on reprocessing keeps getting longer every month
Because Delta Lake tables degrade in read performance over time regardless of design
Because the Regional Manager's new table forces every query to scan twice
Because flat transaction volume always means slower disk I/O
questions.explain: Even with flat daily volume, the total history being reprocessed every night keeps growing month over month, which is what drives runtime up.

questions.q: How does the incremental design break the link between accumulated history and nightly cost?
options: By having Bronze read only files newer than the watermark and Silver merge in only genuinely new rows
By deleting old historical data from bronze.sales_raw once it's a year old
By running the nightly job only once a week instead of daily
By moving all historical data into a separate, unqueried archive table
questions.explain: Once Bronze only ingests new files past the watermark and Silver only merges new/changed rows, nightly cost tracks the size of yesterday's data instead of the whole table's history.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about the illustrative six-months-of-history example?
options: It's a concrete way to reason about the problem's shape, not a real measured benchmark
It's an exact runtime measurement taken from the retail chain's production system
It proves the full-reload design is actually faster than incremental for this data size
It shows that Delta Lake MERGE INTO is slower than a full reload at small scale
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the six-months example as illustrative reasoning about the shape of the problem, not a real benchmark or measurement.
